sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text: 1 Introduction “The two systems [Hamilton’s and Grassmann’s] are not only consistent with one another, but they are actually parts of a larger whole.” — William Kingdon Clifford, 1878 T he design of deep neural networks has long been dominated by a dichotomy: engineering empiricism versus physical mimicry. On one hand, architectures like the Vision Transformer (ViT) [ 1 ] rely on the stacking of engineered blocks (Self-Attention + MLP), a pattern now known as “MetaFormer” [ 2 ] . On the other hand, recent works attempt to ground deep learning in physical laws, modeling networks as discretizations of diffusion processes or fluid dynamics. Beyond Physical Mimicry: A Mathematical Ansatz. While drawing inspiration from physics is valuable, we argue that deep learning architecture design need not be constrained by specific physical laws. Instead, we seek freedom in the abstract landscape of mathematics. We propose a governing equation driven not by a specific physical force, but by algebraic completeness . It represents a mathematically principled Ansatz : that the evolution of latent representations should be driven by the full spectrum of geometric relationships — both scalar alignment (similarity) and bivector structure (orthogonality) — available in the vector space. To this end, we adopt Geometric Algebra (Clifford Algebra) [ 3 , 4 ] as the foundational language of our architecture. Emergent Globality from Local Completeness. A prevailing dogma in modern vision is the necessity of explicit global context (e.g., Global Self-Attention) to capture long-range dependencies. We challenge this view. We posit that global understanding is an emergent property of rigorous local processing . By utilizing Geometric Algebra to maximize the information extraction from local context — creating a dense “entanglement” between a feature and its neighborhood — we implicitly encode global structure without the quadratic cost of global retrieval. Building on this philosophy, we introduce CliffordNet . Unlike standard Transformers that require heavy Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) to perform channel mixing and non-linear transformation, CliffordNet relies on a Dual-Stream Geometric Block powered by the Clifford Geometric Product. One stream captures high-frequency details, while the other aggregates local context; their interaction is modeled via the geometric product to drive feature updates. This interaction mechanism is so expressive that it allows us to drastically reduce, or even completely remove , the FFN component. Crucially, to make this geometric paradigm feasible for high-resolution and high-dimensional backbones, we introduce a Sparse Rolling Interaction strategy. Rather than computing the full [LaTeX: D\times D] D × D D\times D outer product matrix (which scales quadratically with channel dimension), we sample the tangent space via cyclic shifts. This ensures the overall complexity remains linear [LaTeX: \mathcal{O}(N)] 𝒪 ⁡ ( N ) \mathcal{O}(N) in sequence length and [LaTeX: \mathcal{O}(D)] 𝒪 ⁡ ( D ) \mathcal{O}(D) in channel dimension. Our contributions are four-fold: • Mathematical Unification via Clifford Algebra: We reframe visual feature interaction through the lens of Algebraic Completeness . By proposing the Clifford Interaction Ansatz based on the full Geometric Product ( [LaTeX: uv=u\cdot v+u\wedge v] u ​ v = u ⋅ v + u ∧ v uv=u\cdot v+u\wedge v ), we restore the missing spatial structure (bivector) alongside standard scalar similarity, unifying feature gating and geometric flow into a single, theoretically rigorous operation. • Geometric Evolution via Local Context: We formulate deep representation learning asa continuous dynamic evolution governed by a differential equation . Driven by local geometric context (approximated via Laplacian operators), this ansatz bridges physical diffusion processes with neural representation learning, allowing the network to adaptively model feature coherence and structural variation. • Native 2D Topological Fidelity: We challenge the prevailing trend of image serialization (flattening in ViTs, scanning in SSMs). CliffordNet operates natively on isotropic 2D feature grids, utilizing sparse rolling interactions that inherently respect spatial adjacency. This design preserves the intrinsic topology of visual data without requiring complex positional encodings or artificial scanning heuristics. • Paradigm Shift in Efficiency: We challenge the prevailing meta-architecture by demonstrating that heavy Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) are redundant when geometric interactions are sufficiently expressive. Our No-FFN CliffordNet achieves high-level accuracy with only 2.6M parameters, significantly outperforming MobileNetV2, ShuffleNetV2 and ViT-Tiny while establishing a new Pareto frontier for linear-complexity backbones. 0 0 footnotetext: Definition: Algebraic Completeness under Geometric Product. We use the term algebraic completeness to denote the utilization of the full Clifford Geometric Product between two vectors. Standard neural primitives typically utilize only the symmetric scalar component ( [LaTeX: \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v}] 𝐮 ⋅ 𝐯 \mathbf{u}\cdot\mathbf{v} ), discarding the anti-symmetric bivector component ( [LaTeX: \mathbf{u}\wedge\mathbf{v}] 𝐮 ∧ 𝐯 \mathbf{u}\wedge\mathbf{v} ). An architecture is considered algebraically complete in this context if it explicitly models both the coherence (scalar) and structural (bivector) terms of the interaction.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.text: 2 Related Work Geometric & Physics-Inspired Dynamics. Recent research has increasingly integrated geometric priors and physical analogies into deep learning architectures. A pivotal example is RiemannFormer [ 5 ] , which explicitly models the latent space as a Riemannian manifold, employing parallel transport to rectify attention mechanisms. Building upon this geometric foundation, Di Sipio et al. [ 6 ] extended the analogy to General Relativity, interpreting attention weights as a metric that induces curvature in a spacetime where layers represent discrete time steps. While these approaches offer robust theoretical frameworks, they often rely on explicit and computationally intensive manifold operations. CliffordNet shares the dynamic view of treating network depth as temporal evolution but proposes a fundamental paradigm shift in the governing equation. Instead of simulating gravitational curvature or explicitly constructing manifold operators to support attention, we internalize geometry directly into the feature interaction via a Geometric Algebra ansatz . By driving state updates through local geometric conflict (wedge product) and alignment (dot product), we move from “Geometry for Attention” to “Geometry as Computation,” achieving linear complexity without sacrificing theoretical depth . Clifford Neural Networks. The integration of Clifford Algebra into deep learning has gained traction, particularly for tasks requiring geometric symmetry. Existing works [ 7 , 8 ] largely focus on 3D physics simulations and PDE solving, aiming for E(3)-equivariance. However, these architectures typically treat network weights themselves as multivectors, resulting in a combinatorial explosion of parameters (e.g., 16 components for 4D spacetime algebra) and heavy matrix-vector multiplication overhead. In contrast, CliffordNet repurposes Geometric Algebra for general-purpose 2D vision . We do not use Clifford-valued weights; instead, we employ the Geometric Product purely as a lightweight [LaTeX: \mathcal{O}(N)] 𝒪 ⁡ ( N ) \mathcal{O}(N) token interaction mechanism over real-valued feature maps. This design choice allows us to harness the representational density of bivectors without the computational penalty of full algebraic implementations, making it feasible for high-resolution image recognition. Efficient Backbones & Linear Models. The pursuit of efficiency has bifurcated into two paths. On one hand, CNN-based architectures like MobileNetV2 [ 9 ] and ShuffleNetV2 [ 10 ] optimize local operations via depthwise separability and channel shuffling. While efficient, they lack global context modeling. On the other hand, ViT-Tiny [ 11 ] introduces global attention but suffers from quadratic complexity [LaTeX: \mathcal{O}(N^{2})] 𝒪 ⁡ ( N 2 ) \mathcal{O}(N^{2}) , limiting scalability. More recently, linear-complexity models like Mamba (SSM) [ 12 ] and its vision counterparts [ 13 , 14 ] , and RWKV [ 15 ] have emerged, replacing attention with recurrent state-space models. CliffordNet distinguishes itself from these paradigms. Unlike CNNs, it captures long-range dependencies via rolling interactions; unlike ViTs, it maintains strict linear complexity; and unlike SSMs which rely on recurrent state compression, our model relies on algebraic density . Notably, we achieve superior parameter efficiency by rendering the heavy FFN block redundant — a feat not yet demonstrated in CNN or SSM architectures. Native 2D Topology vs. Serialization. A fundamental challenge in modern vision is adapting sequence models to 2D images. ViTs flatten spatial dimensions, relying on global attention to recover lost topological neighborhoods. VMamba [ 14 ] and other SSM-based visual backbones address this by introducing complex scanning trajectories (e.g., cross-scanning) to linearize the image while attempting to preserve 2D causality. While efficient, these scanning heuristics break the continuous manifold structure of the image into discrete 1D paths. In contrast, CliffordNet operates natively on the 2D feature grid. Our geometric context [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}(H)] 𝒞 ⁡ ( H ) \mathcal{C}(H) is instantiated via depth-wise convolution, which inherently respects the spatial locality and isotropy of the image manifold without requiring artificial linearization. We posit that maintaining this topological fidelity is a key factor in our model’s superior performance-efficiency ratio compared to serialization-based approaches.

sections.text: 3 Methodology I n this work, we propose a new family of architectures, the Clifford Algebra Networks (CANs) , which leverage the rich structure of Geometric Algebra to drive feature evolution . While the full algebraic space offers a vast landscape of geometric operations (e.g., multivector convolutions, rotations via rotors), we begin by instantiating the first generation of CANs, which we term CliffordNet . CliffordNet is built upon the most fundamental operation in Clifford Algebra: the Geometric Product ( [LaTeX: uv=u\cdot v+u\wedge v] u ​ v = u ⋅ v + u ∧ v uv=u\cdot v+u\wedge v ). The core hypothesis is that this algebraically complete interaction is sufficient to replace the decoupled mixing stages of standard backbones. In the following part of this section, we present the theoretical foundation of our approach, moving from a general ansatz of feature evolution to the specific instantiation using Clifford Algebra. 3.1 Preliminaries Given an input image [LaTeX: I\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{H}\times\mathbb{W}\times 3}] I ∈ ℝ ℍ × 𝕎 × 3 I\in\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{H}\times\mathbb{W}\times 3} , we apply a patch embedding layer (typically a convolution with kernel size and stride [LaTeX: P] P P ) to project pixel patches into a latent feature space. Crucially, unlike standard Vision Transformers that flatten patches into a 1D sequence, we maintain the 2D spatial arrangement of the tokens throughout the network to facilitate geometric context modeling. We denote the feature state at a given layer as [LaTeX: X\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times w\times D}] X ∈ ℝ h × w × D X\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times w\times D} , where: • [LaTeX: h=\mathbb{H}/P] h = ℍ / P h=\mathbb{H}/P and [LaTeX: w=\mathbb{W}/P] w = 𝕎 / P w=\mathbb{W}/P represent the feature map resolution. • [LaTeX: D] D D denotes the channel (feature) dimension. Upon the initial patch projection, the feature map dimensions [LaTeX: (h\times w\times D)] ( h × w × D ) (h\times w\times D) remain constant throughout all [LaTeX: L] L L layers. This design choice aligns with our theoretical formulation of feature learning as a continuous geometric flow within a fixed phase space, allowing for deep stacking of interaction blocks without spatial information loss. We focus on designing an interaction mechanism that scales linearly with respect to both [LaTeX: N=hw] N = h ​ w N=hw and [LaTeX: D] D D . Throughout this paper, unless otherwise specified, we formulate our equations in a pointwise manner. Let [LaTeX: H(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{D}] H ⁡ ( t ) ∈ ℝ D H(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{D} denote the feature vector of a specific token at layer (time) [LaTeX: t] t t . Operations such as the Clifford product are applied pointwise, while the context operator [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}(\cdot)] 𝒞 ⁡ ( ⋅ ) \mathcal{C}(\cdot) (instantiated via convolution) aggregates spatial information from the local neighborhood of the vector field. 3.2 A General Framework for Feature Evolution We model the layer-wise update of visual features as a continuous dynamic evolution process . Specifically, we hypothesize that the evolution of [LaTeX: H] H H follows a differential equation governed by the interaction between the current state and its local geometric context : [LaTeX: \frac{\partial H}{\partial t}=\mathcal{F}\Big(H,\mathcal{C}(H)\Big)] ∂ H ∂ t = ℱ ⁡ ( H , 𝒞 ⁡ ( H ) ) \frac{\partial H}{\partial t}=\mathcal{F}\Big(H,\mathcal{C}(H)\Big) (1) Here, [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}(H)] 𝒞 ⁡ ( H ) \mathcal{C}(H) represents the contextual field derived from [LaTeX: H] H H , and [LaTeX: \mathcal{F}] ℱ \mathcal{F} is an interaction function coupling the state and its context. This formulation generalizes Residual Networks, where the residual branch approximates the derivative [LaTeX: \frac{\partial H}{\partial t}] ∂ H ∂ t \frac{\partial H}{\partial t} . Our core innovation lies in the specific design of [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}] 𝒞 \mathcal{C} and [LaTeX: \mathcal{F}] ℱ \mathcal{F} to incorporate explicit geometric reasoning. 3.3 The Clifford Interaction Ansatz To fully capture the geometric relationship between the state [LaTeX: H] H H and its context [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}] 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , we define the interaction [LaTeX: \mathcal{F}] ℱ \mathcal{F} using the Clifford Geometric Product 1 1 1 Historical Note: This unification traces back to William Kingdon Clifford (1878), who realized that Hamilton’s algebra of rotations (quaternions, relying on inner products) and Grassmann’s algebra of extensions (subspaces, relying on outer products) were “not only consistent with one another, but parts of a larger whole.” Modern deep learning has inadvertently repeated this historical schism by relying heavily on the dot product (Attention) while neglecting the wedge product. This work aims to restore that algebraic unity. . Standard neural network operations (like dot-product attention) typically project interactions onto a scalar field. We argue that this is geometrically lossy. We define the interaction force as a projection of the full geometric product: [LaTeX: \mathcal{F}(H,\mathcal{C})\coloneqq\mathcal{P}\left(\underbrace{H\cdot\mathcal{C}}_{\text{Coherence}}\oplus\underbrace{H\wedge\mathcal{C}}_{\text{Structure}}\right)] ℱ ⁡ ( H , 𝒞 ) ≔ 𝒫 ⁡ ( H ⋅ 𝒞 ⏟ Coherence ⊕ H ∧ 𝒞 ⏟ Structure ) \mathcal{F}(H,\mathcal{C})\coloneqq\mathcal{P}\left(\underbrace{H\cdot\mathcal{C}}_{\text{Coherence}}\oplus\underbrace{H\wedge\mathcal{C}}_{\text{Structure}}\right) (2) where [LaTeX: \mathcal{P}] 𝒫 \mathcal{P} is a learnable projection operator mapping the multi-grade Clifford space (scalars + bivectors) back to the vector space [LaTeX: \mathbb{R}^{D}] ℝ D \mathbb{R}^{D} . The Generalized Inner Product ( [LaTeX: H\cdot\mathcal{C}] H ⋅ 𝒞 H\cdot\mathcal{C} ): This term captures the alignment or similarity between the feature and its context. The subsequent projection [LaTeX: \mathcal{P}] 𝒫 \mathcal{P} then acts as a learnable contraction operator, fusing the coherent (scalar-derived) and structural (bivector-derived) information back into the fundamental latent dimension. This formulation allows us to harness the algebraic completeness of Clifford theory while maintaining compatibility with standard backpropagation dynamics. 3.4 Context Instantiation via Discrete Laplacian While [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}(H)] 𝒞 ⁡ ( H ) \mathcal{C}(H) could theoretically take many forms, we posit that the most fundamental geometric context for visual data is local variation (e.g., edges and texture gradients). sections.text: 4 Experiments T o empirically validate the efficacy of our proposed Clifford Interaction Ansatz , we conduct extensive evaluations on the CIFAR-100 benchmark. While smaller in scale than ImageNet-1K, CIFAR-100 serves as a rigorous litmus test for architectural efficiency and generalization, particularly for lightweight models, due to its high class diversity and data sparsity (only 500 images per class). We position these experiments as a foundational proof-of-concept : confirming that geometric completeness can yield SOTA performance in resource-constrained regimes, paving the way for future scaling to larger datasets. To ensure a strictly fair comparison with established baselines, we adhere to a rigorous training recipe: 200 epochs, AdamW optimizer, cosine annealing, and regularization (AutoAugment, Random Erasing). For CliffordNet , we additionally employ DropPath [ 17 ] to regulate the training of our geometric interaction layers. In contrast, for classical CNN baselines (e.g., ResNet-18, MobileNetV2), we exclude DropPath to adhere to their canonical training protocols, where regularization is primarily handled by weight decay and data augmentation. By standardizing the optimizer (AdamW) and augmentation pipeline across all models, we ensure a rigorously controlled comparison, evaluating architectural capability under the same modern data regime. Despite relying on unoptimized PyTorch primitives (e.g., rolling), CliffordNet -Nano remains highly competitive in training time while delivering significantly superior accuracy (+1.8% vs. ShuffleNet, +5.5% vs. MobileNetV2) with fewer parameters. Our CliffordNet-Base achieves 78.05% , establishing a new SOTA for models under 4M parameters, surpassing ResNet-18 (11.2M) by a clear margin. The Cost of Geometry vs. Depth. We observe an interesting computational trade-off. Transitioning from Nano (2 shifts) to Fast (5 shifts) improves accuracy by [LaTeX: \sim] ∼ \sim 1.4% but increases training time by [LaTeX: \sim] ∼ \sim 56%. In contrast, adding an FFN layer (Fast [LaTeX: \to] → \to Base) only adds [LaTeX: \sim] ∼ \sim 11% overhead. This indicates that the current bottleneck lies in the geometric sampling density (number of shifts). Potential for Acceleration. It is crucial to note that our current implementation of the “Shifted Geometric Product” relies on standard PyTorch primitives (e.g., torch.roll and slicing), which are memory-bound operations involving redundant data movement. Unlike standard convolutions which benefit from decades of cuDNN optimization, our geometric primitives are unoptimized. This high latency for multi-shift interactions suggests a significant room for improvement . By implementing custom fused CUDA/Triton kernels to perform rolling interactions on-the-fly in registers (avoiding VRAM round-trips), we expect the cost of increasing shifts to become negligible, potentially doubling the throughput of the Base/Fast models in future iterations. Baselines and Architectural Paradigms. We benchmark CliffordNet against three representative efficient architectures. MobileNetV2 [ 9 ] relies on inverted residuals and depth-wise convolutions. ViT-Tiny [ 11 ] represents the isotropic Transformer paradigm, which we evaluate under a constrained parameter budget (Ratio=1). Most notably, we include ShuffleNetV2 [ 10 ] , which exemplifies the pinnacle of structural engineering in CNN design. To mitigate the information blockage caused by group convolutions, ShuffleNetV2 introduces a handcrafted “Channel Shuffle” operation, enabling cross-group information flow while optimizing Memory Access Cost (MAC). CliffordNet outperforms strong baselines across all parameter scales. As shown in Table 2 , while ShuffleNetV2 achieves a strong accuracy of 74.60% through its ingenious engineering heuristics, our CliffordNet-Nano surpasses it by 1.81% with comparable parameters. This result suggests that the implicit channel mixing induced by our mathematically grounded Clifford interaction (via the shifted geometric product) is more effective than the explicit , handcrafted channel shuffling used in traditional efficient CNNs. Our Fast model (Ratio=1) matches the performance of ResNet-18 while using only 24% of the parameters. Even the No-FFN variant achieves 77.63% accuracy, surpassing MobileNetV2 by a large margin, validating our hypothesis that geometric interactions can replace generic MLPs. To prove that our efficiency stems from the architecture and not the dataset, we trained a standard ViT-Tiny with ‘mlp_ratio=1.0‘. The model collapsed to 65.87% accuracy (Table 2 ), whereas CliffordNet maintained 78+%. This confirms that standard attention lacks the geometric density to function without heavy FFNs. Discussion. While Vision Transformers are celebrated for their global receptive field, we argue that this ”global” capability comes at the cost of interaction poverty . The standard dot-product attention compresses the complex, high-dimensional relationship between two tokens into a single scalar ( [LaTeX: \mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}] 𝐪 ⋅ 𝐤 \mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k} ). This operation is fundamentally lossy: it discards the directional and structural information (the bivector component) inherent in the feature space. Consequently, Transformers must rely on heavy, parameter-inefficient FFNs to reconstruct and process these lost feature dimensions. In contrast, CliffordNet takes the opposite approach. We prioritize local algebraic completeness over global scalar matching. By operationalizing the full Geometric Product (and recovering the channel topology via shifted generalized inner products), we extract a dense, information-rich representation from local neighborhoods. Our results show that a network built on rich local interactions can outperform one built on sparse global attention , challenging the prevailing dogma that global is always better. This empirically validates our hypothesis that the Clifford Interaction layer — equipped with multiplicative wedge products and non-linear gating — already possesses sufficient representational capacity, rendering the explicit FFN largely redundant. Table 4 shows that Dot-Only ( 76.91% ) slightly outperforms Wedge-Only ( 76.35% ). However, this comparison reveals a profound geometric insight regarding Diagonal Energy : 1. Crucially, it implicitly encodes feature magnitude or energy (akin to [LaTeX: x_{i}^{2}] x i 2 x_{i}^{2} ), which is fundamental for activation-based deep learning. 2. Despite operating without explicit energy information — effectively fighting with “one hand tied behind its back” — the Wedge-Only variant achieves performance nearly on par with the Dot-Only baseline. This suggests that the structural topology (captured by bivectors) is almost as discriminative as the feature intensity itself. The combination of the two (CliffordNet) thus provides the complete picture: Energy (Dot) + Structure (Wedge). Context Receptive Field & Depth. A baseline using a single [LaTeX: 3\times 3] 3 × 3 3\times 3 depth-wise convolution achieves 77.05% . This factorization provides a dual benefit: It reduces the parameter count of the context stream. sections.text: 5 Discussion I n this section, we analyze the theoretical implications of our empirical findings, interpreting why a pure geometric framework can outperform established architectural paradigms, and positioning CliffordNet within the broader landscape of geometric deep learning. 5.1 Why does the “No-FFN” Paradigm Work? The most counter-intuitive finding of this work is that CliffordNet achieves a high performance (77.63% on CIFAR-100) even without Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs), a component previously considered indispensable in MetaFormer architectures for channel mixing and non-linearity. We attribute this success to the Algebraic Density of the Clifford Interaction: • Internalized Non-linearity: In standard ViTs, the Attention mechanism is primarily a linear aggregation (post-softmax), necessitating a heavy FFN ( [LaTeX: \text{ratio}=4] ratio = 4 \text{ratio}=4 ) to provide feature transformation capacity. In contrast, our Clifford Geometric Product inherently involves multiplicative second-order terms (the bivector [LaTeX: u\wedge v] u ∧ v u\wedge v and scalar [LaTeX: u\odot v] u ⊙ v u\odot v ). When combined with the non-linear GGR gating, the interaction layer itself acts as a powerful function approximator. The geometric interaction effectively “internalizes” the complexity typically delegated to external MLPs. • Structured vs. Brute-force Mixing: An FFN performs dense, agnostic channel mixing via large matrix multiplications. Our Shifted Geometric Product performs structured mixing based on the ring topology of the feature space. Our results suggest that this geometrically constrained mixing is more sample-efficient than the brute-force connectivity of large MLPs, allowing the network to perform high-level reasoning with significantly fewer parameters. 5.2 Theoretical View: A Geometric Reaction-Diffusion System While the Laplacian term [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}\coloneqq\Delta H] 𝒞 ≔ Δ ​ H \mathcal{C}\coloneqq\Delta H suggests a connection to heat diffusion (smoothing), the presence of the geometric product introduces a more complex dynamic, closely resembling a Geometric Reaction-Diffusion System . In mathematical biology, Turing patterns arise from the interplay between diffusion (spreading) and reaction (local non-linear interaction). CliffordNet can be interpreted as a high-dimensional generalization of this morphogenetic process: • Anisotropic Diffusion ( [LaTeX: H\cdot\mathcal{C}] H ⋅ 𝒞 H\cdot\mathcal{C} ): The scalar term, implemented as a generalized inner product, acts as a coherence-based gating mechanism. It functions effectively as anisotropic diffusion , smoothing out noise in homogeneous regions where features align with their context, thereby stabilizing the learning dynamics. • Geometric Reaction ( [LaTeX: H\wedge\mathcal{C}] H ∧ 𝒞 H\wedge\mathcal{C} ): The bivector term introduces a rotational “reaction” force. Unlike simple scalar reactions, this Clifford interaction generates geometric vorticity . It preserves and enhances structural boundaries (edges) where the feature vector diverges orthogonally from its local context, counteracting the smoothing effects of diffusion. This perspective offers a compelling explanation for the network’s effectiveness without FFNs: the architecture evolves raw pixel data into structured semantic representations through a cascade of geometric pattern formation steps, mirroring the emergence of complex structures in nature. 5.3 Hardware-Aware Geometric Approximation Our implementation reflects a philosophy of Pragmatic Platonism : bridging ideal mathematical structures with hardware realities. • Factorized Linear Laplacian: While the context [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}(H)] 𝒞 ⁡ ( H ) \mathcal{C}(H) represents a continuous Laplacian operator, we approximate it via a stack of two [LaTeX: 3\times 3] 3 × 3 3\times 3 depth-wise convolutions. sections.text: 6 Conclusion and Future Work W e presented the Clifford Algebra Network (CAN) , a vision backbone grounded in algebraic completeness rather than heuristic engineering. By operationalizing the Clifford Geometric Product as a linear-complexity token mixer, we demonstrated that FFNs can be rendered redundant, leading to a new class of highly efficient and geometrically interpretable models. By adhering to the mathematical principle of algebraic completeness , we derived a geometric interaction layer that is efficient, robust, and expressive. Our empirical results — particularly the success of the “No-FFN” variant — suggest that with the right geometric priors, deep learning models can be significantly simplified, potentially to the point where geometry is all you need . The name ”Clifford Algebra Network” is deliberate: our current implementation only scratches the surface of what is possible within this rich mathematical framework. We highlight several promising avenues for future research: • Scaling to Large-Scale Data: We plan to validate CliffordNet on ImageNet-1K and ImageNet-21K. A key open question is whether the “No-FFN” paradigm maintains its efficacy when the data scale increases by orders of magnitude, or if the geometric interaction requires wider channel mixing to capture the diversity of real-world scenes. • Dense Prediction Tasks: Due to its strict linear complexity [LaTeX: \mathcal{O}(N)] 𝒪 ⁡ ( N ) \mathcal{O}(N) , CliffordNet is theoretically ideal for high-resolution tasks such as semantic segmentation and object detection. Unlike standard ViTs that struggle with quadratic costs at high resolutions, our architecture can process fine-grained feature maps (e.g., [LaTeX: 1024\times 1024] 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 ) efficiently, making it a strong candidate for next-generation dense vision backbones. • Higher-Order Geometric Products: Our model utilizes the product of two vectors (Grade 1 [LaTeX: \times] × \times Grade 1), which generates scalars (Grade 0) and bivectors (Grade 2). Future versions of CAN could explore interactions with higher-order geometric entities, such as the product of a vector and a bivector ( [LaTeX: v\cdot(u\wedge w)] v ⋅ ( u ∧ w ) v\cdot(u\wedge w) ). This would allow the network to model more complex volumetric or rotational dynamics, potentially benefiting 3D vision and video understanding. • Adaptive Geometric Topology: Currently, our sparse rolling mechanism employs a simple, heuristic set of fixed offsets (e.g., exponential powers), applied uniformly to both the inner (Dot) and exterior (Wedge) product pathways. This assumes that feature coherence and structural contrast operate at identical channel distances, which may not be optimal. Future work could explore decoupling these interaction topologies — finding distinct shift sets tailored for scalar vs. bivector interactions — or introducing learnable/adaptive shifts to dynamically discover the optimal geometric connectivity for specific tasks. This can be viewed as learning the connection coefficients on the feature manifold. • Intrinsic Manifold Learning: Currently, our approach operates on an embedding of the geometric product. Future work could explore intrinsic manifold operations, such as defining metrics based on geodesic distances on the Grassmannian or integrating parallel transport (as explored in RiemannFormer [ 5 ] ), to further tighten the connection between differential geometry and representation learning. • Geometric Attention Augmentation: Our “Shifted Generalized Inner Product” reveals a limitation in standard Self-Attention: the scalar dot product ( [LaTeX: \mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k}] 𝐪 ⋅ 𝐤 \mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{k} ) ignores channel topology. We envision extending this concept to Transformers by introducing Geometric Multi-Head Attention , where attention heads are defined not by learned projections, but by cyclic channel shifts. Combined with sparse attention mechanisms (e.g., windowing), this could inject rich geometric inductive biases into ViTs without incurring quadratic costs. • Hardware-Aware Optimization: While our algorithmic complexity is strictly linear, our current implementation relies on standard PyTorch primitives (e.g., torch.roll ) which involve memory-bound permutation and broadcasting. We plan to develop custom fused CUDA/Triton kernels to perform the rolling interaction and geometric product on-the-fly within registers. This would eliminate intermediate memory I/O, potentially delivering another [LaTeX: 2\times] 2 × 2\times – [LaTeX: 3\times] 3 × 3\times wall-clock speedup and bridging the engineering gap with highly optimized convolution libraries (cuDNN). • Geometric Multi-Modal Fusion: Beyond visual backbones, the algebraic structure of CliffordNet offers a universal interface for multi-modal learning (e.g., Vision-Language models). By treating [LaTeX: H] H H and [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}] 𝒞 \mathcal{C} as heterogeneous modalities (e.g., Image and Text tokens), the Clifford Geometric Product extends standard Cross-Attention (scalar alignment) to include Cross-Modal Bivectors (wedge product). This implies a new fusion paradigm where modalities are not just aligned, but geometrically composed into higher-order semantic planes, potentially offering richer representations for generative tasks. • Data-Dependent Manifold Geometry: Currently, our Laplacian context [LaTeX: \mathcal{C}(H)] 𝒞 ⁡ ( H ) \mathcal{C}(H) relies on static convolution kernels, implying a fixed geometric prior for all images. A compelling direction, inspired by RiemannFormer [ 5 ] , is to make the metric structure dynamic . By formulating the LBO as a function of the input features themselves (e.g., via dynamic convolutions or local attention), we could model a coupled system where “matter tells space how to curve” (features define the metric) and “space tells matter how to move” (the metric guides the Clifford flow). • Symplectic Geometric Flow: The prominence of the wedge product ( [LaTeX: H\wedge\mathcal{C}] H ∧ 𝒞 H\wedge\mathcal{C} ) suggests a deep connection to Symplectic Geometry , where dynamics are governed by a skew-symmetric symplectic form.
